name: Dönnhoff Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle Riesling Spätlese 2015
text:
## Dönnhoff Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle Riesling Spätlese 2015

**The story.** The Dönnhoff family came to the [Nahe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahe_%28wine_region%29) valley about 250 years ago and settled in the small village of [Oberhausen an der Nahe](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Weingut+D%C3%B6nnhoff,+Oberhausen+an+der+Nahe,+Germany&t=k), running a traditional farm with livestock, vegetable gardens and some vines. Hermann Dönnhoff started the wine estate in the 1920s. Helmut Dönnhoff took over from his father in 1966, when there were just four hectares of vines; in 1971 the farmland was sold, and Helmut turned his whole attention to quality wine. The estate has grown to about 25 hectares, which father and son say is as big as they ever want to be ([Skurnik Wines](https://www.skurnik.com/producer/donnhoff/)). Hugh Johnson praised Helmut's "fanatical commitment to quality, and a remarkable natural talent for winemaking", and Robert Parker called him a "superstar" ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%C3%B6nnhoff)).

His son Cornelius trained at Dr. Heger in Baden, studied in Bad Kreuznach, worked in New Zealand and Australia, and became cellarmaster in 2007. In 2014 [Stuart Pigott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuart_Pigott) named him Winemaker of the Year in the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung ([CellarHand](https://cellarhand.com.au/producers/donnhoff/)). The family motto: "Das ganze Ding muss klingen", the whole thing must ring true; and "winemaking alone cannot bring quality; it can only retain the available quality" ([Skurnik Wines](https://www.skurnik.com/producer/donnhoff/)).

**In the vineyard and cellar.** The Nahe is a dry region, but Dönnhoff never irrigates, so the vines root deep; the soil is mulched with straw and compost. The vines are trained low to catch the warmth of the stony topsoil, and everything is picked by hand in two or three passes. The grapes are pressed within three hours of picking, and the wines ferment spontaneously in traditional German oak casks (1,200-litre *Stück* and 2,400-litre *Doppelstück*) or stainless steel ([Skurnik Wines](https://www.skurnik.com/producer/donnhoff/)).

**The region.** The Nahe is a small region along the river [Nahe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahe_%28Rhine%29), with very varied soils born of its volcanic past. Although wine was made here in Roman times and the village of Monzingen was named as a wine village in 778, the Nahe was only defined as a region by the 1971 German wine law; before that its wines were sold as plain "Rhine wine". Today its best Rieslings are rated on a par with the Mosel and Rheingau ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahe_%28wine_region%29)).

**What Spätlese means.** [Spätlese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_wine_classification) means "late harvest": in Germany's ripeness-based system, the wine's category depends on how ripe the grapes were at picking. At Dönnhoff, Spätlese is a classic fruity, sweet style, with residual sugar balanced by high acidity, and it ages for decades.

**The vineyard: Hermannshöhle.** The Hermannshöhle lies at [Niederhausen](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Hermannsh%C3%B6hle,+Niederhausen,+Germany&t=k), where the village sits on a south-facing slope above a dammed, 120-metre-wide stretch of the river Nahe, on the edge of the [Hunsrück](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hunsr%C3%BCck) hills ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niederhausen)). It is Dönnhoff's most famous site, and Stephan Reinhardt of the Wine Advocate writes that "there is no other Riesling in the Nahe that has such nobly aristocratic attitude" ([Bordeaux Index](https://bordeauxindex.com/fine-wine/germany/nahe/donhs-2015)).

**The vintage.** [Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson)'s [Germany vintage chart](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/learn/vintages/germany) says 2015 yields across the country met the ten-year average, though they varied by region, with the [Mosel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosel_%28wine_region%29) especially promising and the [Rheingau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rheingau_%28wine_region%29) tipped for excellence; Rieslings were "very good but rarely exciting". Dönnhoff's 2015s were the exception: Reinhardt called this "one of the finest Spätlese Rieslings you can buy from this vintage".

**What the critics say for 2015.**
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 95** (Stephan Reinhardt, October 2016, as listed by [Bordeaux Index](https://bordeauxindex.com/fine-wine/germany/nahe/donhs-2015)). "An aristocratic bouquet of coolish, flinty slate and citrus perfume"; great complexity; highly elegant, with "seamless, silky texture", very salty, full of finesse and tension. "A great, perfectly balanced Spätlese."
- The same critic, writing about the 2015 Hermannshöhle Auslese, said it shares the Spätlese's "noble aristocracy"; David Schildknecht (Vinous) found that the Auslese "misses the dynamic or the focus of its Spätlese counterpart" ([Bordeaux Index](https://bordeauxindex.com/fine-wine/germany/nahe/donha-2015)). In other words, your Spätlese may be the more thrilling of the two.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 93.3** (from your CellarTracker list), the highest-scored white in this batch.

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is eleven years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2022 to 2060. Spätlese Riesling of this quality lives for decades: it is in its first drinking window now, with the baby fat gone and slate, citrus, peach and salt coming through, and it will keep evolving towards honeyed, petrol-tinged complexity for 30 years or more. Open one now; keep the rest.

**Serving.** Serve chilled, about 8 to 10°C, in a white wine glass. Young Spätlese can be opened and poured; older bottles benefit from 20 to 30 minutes in the glass. An opened bottle keeps for several days in the fridge, and often improves.

**Food.** The sweetness and high acidity of Spätlese make it brilliant with spicy food: Thai green curry, Sichuan dishes, Indian food, or Vietnamese pork. It also loves roast pork or duck with fruit, [smoked salmon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoked_salmon), crab, and soft cheeses; and it is lovely on its own as an aperitif.

**Value and where to buy.** BC Liquor carries Dönnhoff's 2022 Niederhäuser Hermannshöhle Riesling Auslese Gold Cap at $91.99. For Germany's top estates, Dönnhoff's Spätlesen are remarkably fairly priced.

**From the history books**
- **Roman roots.** The Nahe was populated in Roman times, and Monzingen was recorded as a wine village in 778 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahe_%28wine_region%29)). [Niederhausen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niederhausen), home of the Hermannshöhle, was first mentioned in 1238, though Roman finds show it was settled around AD 200 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niederhausen)).
- **Late to the vine, then famous.** The Nahe was one of the last German regions to plant vines widely, nearly six centuries after the Romans first farmed the Mosel. In the 19th century it was counted among Germany's finest regions, before falling behind after the two world wars ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahe_%28wine_region%29)).
- **The VDP.** Dönnhoff belongs to the VDP, the association of Germany's top estates, organised since 1910, which classifies the best vineyards as Grosse Lage (grand cru) using 19th-century Prussian tax maps ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_wine_classification)).

**Curious details**
- **"No one knows the Nahe, but everyone knows Dönnhoff."** That's what they say in the United States, according to the estate's Australian importer ([CellarHand](https://cellarhand.com.au/producers/donnhoff/)).
- **A village of 400.** Oberhausen, home of one of Germany's most famous estates, has a population of about 400 ([CellarHand](https://cellarhand.com.au/producers/donnhoff/)).
- **A volcanic patchwork.** The Nahe's soils are unusually varied because of the region's volcanic origins ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nahe_%28wine_region%29)).
